questions.q: What is the common gap this lesson describes between application code and database changes?
options: Database changes are always automatically committed to Git by SQL Server
There is no meaningful difference between application code and DDL
SSMS automatically version-controls every change you make
Application code is routinely kept in Git with history and authorship, while database changes are often made ad hoc with no diff or record
questions.explain: The database is routinely the exception to source control — changes get made directly with no diff, author, or rollback point.

questions.q: Why does DDL belong in source control, per this lesson?
options: Because DDL is text, just like application code, and can be tracked, diffed, and reviewed the same way
Because Git can only store binary files
Because DDL cannot be scripted out of SSMS
Because SQL Server requires it to run
questions.explain: CREATE TABLE, CREATE PROCEDURE, and similar statements are just text — the same kind of artifact source control already handles well.

questions.q: What is a key limitation of the plain-scripts-in-Git approach to database source control?
options: Git cannot store .sql files
It requires SQL Server Enterprise Edition
Nothing enforces that a live change is actually committed — the repo can silently drift from reality
It automatically deploys every commit to production
questions.explain: Without a database project's build validation and process discipline, a DBA can make a live change and simply forget to commit the matching script.

questions.q: What is an SSDT database project?
options: A cloud-only Azure SQL Database feature
A Visual Studio project representing a database's intended schema as individual scripted object files, which can build and validate before deployment
A GUI tool for browsing table data
A backup format for disaster recovery
questions.explain: SSDT formalizes scripted objects into a real project with build validation, producing a DACPAC for deployment.

questions.q: In an SSDT database project workflow, what becomes the source of truth for the schema?
options: The most recent SSMS session
The DBA's memory of past changes
The database project itself — changes are made there first, then deployed to the live database
Whatever the production database currently looks like
questions.explain: SSDT inverts the ad hoc model: the project represents the intended schema, and deployment pushes that intent to the database, not the other way around.
